query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy nanoalloys used for high-temperature applications, stability is primarily governed by the temperature‐dependent rate of surface atomic diffusion; once a critical temperature is exceeded, enhanced surface diffusion leads to elemental segregation and phase separation that counteracts the stabilizing effect of high configurational entropy.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoscale, single-phase solid-solution high-entropy nanoalloys with uniformly dispersed multiple principal elements.
generation.intervention: Implement a diffusion-suppressing modification by incorporating a minor alloying addition or surface passivation to reduce surface atomic mobility.
generation.conditions: High-temperature aging in an inert atmosphere within a defined temperature window (approximately 600°C to 1000°C) where atomic diffusion processes are significantly activated.
generation.structural_mediator: Controlled evolution of surface composition via slight alloying changes that slow down atomic jump rates and delay surface segregation.
generation.mechanism: At moderate temperatures, high configurational entropy maintains a well-mixed state; however, as temperature increases, enhanced surface and grain-boundary diffusion promotes local elemental segregation, leading to phase separation and structural degradation unless diffusion is mitigated through targeted modifications.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to unmodified nanoalloys, samples with diffusion-suppressing modifications will exhibit significantly less elemental segregation and maintain a more uniform structure under high-temperature aging.
generation.baseline: Standard high-entropy nanoalloys without any specific surface diffusion suppression measures.
generation.boundary: This prediction applies within the temperature range above the onset of accelerated diffusion (around 600°C) and below the melting or catastrophic phase transformation temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in segregation and the precise critical temperature for the onset of rapid diffusion remain uncertain and require experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy nanoalloy samples: one with the standard composition and one modified by a minor alloying addition or surface passivation to reduce surface diffusion. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature aging between 600°C and 1000°C in an inert atmosphere. Monitor the structural and chemical evolution in situ using high-resolution TEM and EDS.
measurements: Quantification of elemental segregation levels (via EDS mapping)
Assessment of phase uniformity and microstructural changes (via in situ TEM or XRD)
Comparison of degradation rates between modified and unmodified samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the modified and baseline samples show similar degrees of elemental segregation and structural degradation under high-temperature aging, the hypothesis attributing stability primarily to slowed diffusion kinetics is falsified.

The inherent chemical complexity in compositionally complex materials poses challenges for modeling atomic diffusion and the resulting formation of chemically ordered structures. Here, we introduce a neural network kinetics (NNK) scheme that predicts and simulates diffusion-induced chemical and structural evolution in complex concentrated chemical environments. The framework is grounded on efficient on-lattice structure and chemistry representation combined with artificial neural networks, enabling precise prediction of all path-dependent migration barriers and individual atom jumps. To demonstrate the method, we study the temperature-dependent local chemical ordering in a refractory NbMoTa alloy and reveal a critical temperature at which the B2 order reaches a maximum. The atomic jump randomness map exhibits the highest diffusion heterogeneity (multiplicity) in the vicinity of this characteristic temperature, which is closely related to chemical ordering and B2 structure formation. The structural stability of the prototype CoCrFeMnNi HEA has been extensively studied in a wide temperature range from 55 K to its melting temperature of ∼1,600 K at ambient pressure but to our knowledge, no polymorphic transition has been observed. Conversely, high-pressure studies remain a virgin area in HEAs. In this work, using in situ high-pressure XRD techniques, we observed the first polymorphic transition from fcc to hcp in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA, as shown in Fig. 1c. Therefore, some critical questions are how and why can an hcp HEA form at high-pressure and can it be maintained at ambient conditions? According to the d-spacing of the main reflections of both fcc and hcp (that is, (111) and (220) of fcc, and (100), (002), (101) and (110) of hcp, as a function of pressure shown in Fig. 2a), it is clear that the hcp-(002) and hcp-(110) planes inherit the fcc-(111) and fcc-(220) planes, respectively. In addition, Fig. 2b shows no obvious volume collapse during the transition; both the fcc and hcp phases seem to have almost the same volume per atom and bulk modulus. One of the major challenges of near-equiatomic NiTi shape memory alloys is their limitation for high-temperature applications. To overcome this barrier, researchers have tried to enhance the transformation temperatures by addition of alloying elements or even by introducing the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs). In this study, the CuNiHfTiZr HEAs were developed for high-temperature shape memory effect. Based on their solubility and electron configurations, the alloying elements are divided into two groups, (CuNi)50 and (HfTiZr)50. The content of Cu in (CuNi)50 is modulated to investigate the influences of Cu on martensitic transformation of the HEAs by studying structural evolution and transformation behavior. The results of x-ray diffraction and thermal expansion tests revealed that Cu15Ni35Hf16.67Ti16.67Zr16.67 possesses high transformation temperature, narrow hysteresis temperature loops, and good dimensional stability within this HEA system.

chosen.lever: surface composition evolution and diffusion kinetics
chosen.technique: in situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
chosen.conditions: a controlled temperature program from 600°C to 1000°C in an inert gas environment that mimics high-temperature service conditions
chosen.why: Previous work on high-entropy alloys often focused on bulk or static measurements while neglecting the dynamic surface diffusion and chemical segregation mechanisms at the nanoscale. This controlled experiment directly inverts the gap by actively varying temperature and composition to distinguish whether rapid surface diffusion governs the loss of structural and chemical stability.

frame.system: High-entropy nanoalloys designed for high-temperature applications, initially in a nanoscale solid-solution state with multiple principal elemental components.
frame.goal: To understand the mechanisms governing the structural and chemical stability—specifically, how atomic interactions, diffusion kinetics, and configurational entropy interplay at elevated temperatures.
frame.limitation: The fundamental drivers of stability in these nanoalloys remain ambiguous: it is not clear whether high configurational entropy alone is sufficient to maintain the stable single-phase structure at high temperatures or if kinetic factors (such as enhanced surface diffusion and segregation) ultimately dictate degradation.
root_cause_cues: what governs structural and chemical stability
constraints: Operating at high temperatures where diffusion processes are activated
Maintaining nanoscale dimensions where surface effects are pronounced
Requiring a controlled comparison to distinguish between entropy stabilization and kinetic segregation mechanisms
frame.regime: High-temperature regime (approaching or exceeding typical service temperatures for these alloys), with nanoscale feature sizes that amplify diffusion and surface segregation effects.
prior_attempts: Studies relying chiefly on equilibrium phase diagrams or compositional entropy metrics have inadequately accounted for kinetic processes (such as atomic diffusion and surface segregation) that become critical at elevated temperatures.
frame.understanding: The testable mechanistic hypothesis is that in high-entropy nanoalloys, structural and chemical stability is predominantly governed by the temperature‐dependent rate of atomic diffusion and associated surface or interface segregation. Specifically, although the high configurational entropy favors a single-phase solid solution at moderate temperatures, once a critical temperature is surpassed, accelerated diffusion leads to local elemental segregation and phase separation, undermining stability. A controlled comparison could involve preparing two sets of nanoalloy samples: one with an alloy design that inherently retards surface diffusion (e.g., via grain size refinement or surface passivation) and another with a conventional design. Under identical high-temperature aging conditions, the diffusion-suppressed nanoalloys are predicted to exhibit significantly less chemical segregation and structural degradation relative to the baseline. This prediction holds within a defined temperature window (above the onset of accelerated diffusion but below total melting or catastrophic phase transformation temperatures). Supporting evidence comes from earlier observations in bulk high-entropy alloys where kinetic limitations were linked to improved phase stability, although such effects are amplified at the nanoscale. A falsifying outcome would be if both sample sets, irrespective of their design to modulate diffusion barriers, display equivalent levels of phase segregation and structural instability upon thermal stressing, thereby implying that factors other than diffusion kinetics (or the interplay with configurational entropy) are dominant.

decision.trend: Early work on high-entropy nanoalloys (e.g. PMC4510962) established that nanoscale architectures (thin films, micropillars) can exhibit remarkable high-temperature stability—a result largely interpreted from equilibrium and phase-diagram perspectives. Subsequent studies (PMC7311485) revealed that, at the nanoscale, grain size and near‐surface evolution (including dynamic amorphization) play an important role, hinting that diffusion processes and surface segregation might contribute to stability. Later in situ investigations (PMC8011962) further highlighted that deformation and thermal activation can trigger crystalline‐to‐amorphous transitions by accumulating local stresses and facilitating atomic mobility at grain boundaries. Overall, the research trajectory has moved from attributing stability solely to configurational entropy towards recognizing that temperature‐activated atomic diffusion and surface/interface segregation become critical at high temperatures.
decision.unsolved: Despite evidence for both high configurational entropy and kinetic diffusion processes contributing to stability, it remains unresolved whether the observed structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys at elevated temperatures is primarily governed by slowed diffusion or by entropy stabilization. In particular, a clear, controlled comparison that isolates the influence of surface diffusion kinetics versus equilibrium entropy considerations within the critical temperature window has yet to be achieved.
decision.lever: surface composition evolution via controlled alloying
decision.why: Given the trend from equilibrium-based designs to experiments revealing the critical role of kinetic processes and near-surface structural evolution, the next logical step is a controlled variable experiment. By intentionally modifying surface composition—such as through a minor alloying addition or surface passivation—the research can directly test how slowing surface atomic diffusion impacts segregation and phase stability under a controlled temperature ramp (600°C to 1000°C in an inert atmosphere). This approach directly addresses the open question by distinguishing whether enhanced stability arises from entropy effects or from diffusion-limited segregation, and it occupies the niche of probing the mechanistic origins of stability through in situ high-resolution TEM and EDS characterization.
